newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania on right track to NATO-U.S. Congressman.
newsitem.headline: Romania on right track to NATO-U.S. Congressman.

text.p: A senior U.S. Congressman said on Thursday that Romania's hopes for early admission to NATO had been boosted by last November's elections in which centrists took over from ex-communists.

"Romania's joining NATO is on the table because Romania had free, open and democratic elections and the government accepts the rights of all religious groups and ethnic minorities," Tom Lantos, a California Democrat, told a news conference.
"I'll personally support Romania being invited simultaneously with Hungary, the Czech Republic, Poland and Slovenia to begin discussions leading to NATO membership."

Lantos, co-chairman of the the Bipartisan Congressional Human Rights Caucus, an umbrella group of the Congress monitoring human rights, travelled on to Budapest after stops in Romania and the former Soviet republic of Ukraine.

Romania seeks Western assurances that it stands a chance to beat the odds and join frontrunners Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic in the Alliance's first eastward expansion, to be decided at a July summit in Madrid.
Romania and Slovenia are viewed as less likely contenders, but have recently gained ground on the leaders.
During his two-day visit, the Hungarian-born Lantos had talks with the new centrist coalition leadership, which includes members of Romania's large ethnic Hungarian community.
He praised Bucharest and Budapest for a treaty signed last September patching up old rifts between the ex-communist neighbours over borders and ethnic minorities.
"This treaty contributes to the stability of the region, as will the treaty between Romania and Ukraine. NATO has no intention of inviting ethnic or national disputes," he said.

Romanian and Ukrainian diplomats resumed talks this month on a long-delayed post-communist accord. The accord is stalled over Bucharest's insistence that Kiev atone for loss of Romanian lands to the Kremlin under the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact which carved up large swathes of Eastern Europe.
Lantos said Moscow's vehement opposition to NATO's expansion was unjustified.

"Russia has no reason whatsoever to be concerned with the admission of new states into NATO, just the contrary," he said. "As we expand NATO we expand the pattern of stability from Western Europe to central and Eastern Europe."
